utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The case number is IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the Defence, the first Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the second Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else present in this courtroom. This week we will be hearing a number of so-called international witnesses, and on Friday the hearing will be one during which we will be discussing the documents. Mr. Withopf, who do we have today according to your memorandum? It's Mr. Baggesen; isn't that correct? 8 WITHOPF: That's correct, Mr. President. The Prosecution will call Mr. Lars Baggesen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Usher, could you bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I would like to check that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying into your language. If that is the case, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can read you loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. Before you take -- in order for you to be able to take the solemn declaration, I would like you to tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Lars Baggesen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Copenhagen, the 22nd of January, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm Danish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current position? You're wearing a uniform. Which army are you a member of and what is your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a major in the Danish Army, and just now I am staff officer at Danish Home Guard Command. That's on general staff level. And I'm responsible for cooperation with the Baltic countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what position did you hold? That's over ten years ago now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the ECMM in the period from April until end June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rank did you hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In ECMM, we didn't have any ranks, but my rank in Denmark in the Danish Army was captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the third time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the third time. To the extent that you can remember this, can you tell us which case you testified in and were you called as a witness for the Prosecution or for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called for the Prosecution in the case against Colonel Blaskic, and later on in the case against Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the solemn declaration. The usher will show the text to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may sit down. As this is the third time that you will be testifying before this Tribunal, you are used to giving testimony; nevertheless, I would like to remind you of certain factors. You will first have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. They are to your right. They will be conducting what we call their examination-in-chief. Once they have completed the examination-in-chief, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination. Once they have concluded their cross-examination, the Prosecution may re-examine you. And the three Judges, who are sitting before you, may at any time during this proceedings ask you questions either to clarify some of the answers you have given or in order to obtain information about certain aspects of your testimony that didn't form part of the answers to the questions put to you. As you are used to such hearings, you know that it is necessary to answer as precisely and extensively as possible, as the Judges don't have your written statement, and it is therefore your oral testimony that will be contributing to the determination of the truth. If there are any questions that you don't understand, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. These are purely academic issues that I'm now going to mention, but you have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you shouldn't give false testimony. If a witness gives false testimony, a witness could be punished as a result. And if a witness's testimony could at a subsequent date be used against the witness, in such a case a witness may refuse to answer such a question. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber could compel the witness to answer the question. In such a case, the Trial Chamber guarantees a form of immunity for the witness. This is a provision contained in the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So this is roughly speaking how your testimony will proceed. If you encounter any difficulties, please inform the Trial Chamber of this. You will be testifying today, and I don't think it will be necessary for you to appear in the courtroom tomorrow. Without wasting any more time, I will let the Prosecution take the floor. They will conduct their examination-in-chief. Now, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber briefly summarise your military career within the Danish Army with an emphasise on any deployments abroad.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. I started my military career in 1976, where I started with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. my national service in the Danish Army, and I have been in the army since then. I was promoted as officer in 1978, as an infantry officer. Later on I was educated in the Cavalry and the Reconnaissance Unit. My time as an officer has been a mix of commanding units and staff duties, and the staff duties has always been as -- until my present job, has always been as a -- an intelligence officer at battalion and brigade level. I participated in different missions. In 1980-1981, I was participating in the conflict at Cyprus, where I was a member of UNFICYP, the forces in Cyprus, where I was a staff officer in the Danish Battalion. In 1993, as you know, I was a member of the ECMM in Central Bosnia, and in 2001 I was a G2 at the French Brigade headquarters in KFOR in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I know you already mentioned it, but what was your military rank in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: In 1993, I had a military rank as captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what's your military rank today?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Today I'm major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, you already mentioned that you got training as an intelligence officer. Can you please very briefly elaborate on what sort of training you received.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The sort of training we received as intelligence officer, for my part it was during the Cold War, so we were trained in analysing the Warsaw Pact, how their tactics was, what type of materiel they had, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, based on this training, would it be fair to say that you were trained a professional and an experienced intelligence officer and military observer?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned that you had a number of commanding positions over the years. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber at what levels and how many troops you have commanded.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: My first command was platoon commander, where I had 35 soldiers. And my latest command was as a battalion commander, where I had 1.700 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe your current duties within the Danish Army.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: My current duties are as a staff officer in the Danish Home Guard Command. That's on the general staff level. And I am responsible for the cooperation with the Baltic countries, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. I'm responsible for the cooperation and helping the three countries to build up a volunteer force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the last issue I wish to address in this context, Major: Do you plan to go back to the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I know that the army have plans for that, and I am going back to Kosovo this autumn again as a G2 at the French Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I see my colleague from the Defence side on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, page 7, line 9, I would just like the witness to confirm the number he mentioned. The number that appears in the transcript is 1.700. I would just like the witness to confirm whether the number is 1.700 or 700.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Did he command a battalion of 1.700 men or of 700 men? Witness, you said that you were in command of a battalion composed of a certain number of men. How many men exactly

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct in the transcript. It was 1.700 men. And I used the -- the size of the unit as a battalion in the Home Guard, called a Home Guard district. But it's normally battalion level but it's a very big unit with, in this case, 17 companies, including two police companies, one headquarter company, and the rest were infantry companies. But it was not a battalion as you know it in the regular army but in the volunteer defence in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major, for the clarification and confirmation. Let's move to a different issue, your deployment with ECMM in Central Bosnia. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber when you were deployed in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I was deployed to Bosnia the 21st of March, and I stayed in Central Bosnia until end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And we are talking March to June 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where in Bosnia were you deployed?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I was deployed to the regional centre in Zenica, and we had our headquarters at Hotel Internacional.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Hotel Internacional, how far away is it from the 3rd Corps Command -- or was it away from the 3rd Corps Command in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I would say within 1.000 metres, in that environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber inform us about your mission and the purpose of your mission.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As the mission for the ECMM was to -- to see -- to make cease-fires, to make the two parties, the HVO and the BiH, try to have them cooperating again. We had to investigate in -- in different incidents, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was your position between March and July 1993 within the regional centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: In the beginning, from April and the first months, I was a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission, a commission in which there were -- the commission was chaired by ECMM. We were, including the chairman, three members from ECMM, and then there were three members from HVO and three members for army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And in addition to your duties connected to the Busovaca Joint Commission, what else did you do?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: After I was a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission, the commission was closed and renamed and had another task. I was sent to another area of Central Bosnia. I was promoted to team leader, and my new area of responsibility was the area of Zepce, Zavidovici, and Maglaj. And a little later I had increased my area, so I had the Kakanj and Visoko area as well. And after that, in -- in June - I think it was the 10th of June - I was promoted to chairman for the joint humanitarian commission, that -- which task was to release all detained persons in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All these positions, Major, were all these positions you just detailed, were they all within your assignment to the ECMM regional centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who at the time was the head of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The head of the regional centre Zenica was Jean-Pierre Thebault, from France.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please give us the names of your colleagues within the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The centre was, as I told you, headed by Jean-Pierre Thebault, and then we had in the staff if -- we had a Spanish monitor, Juan Valentin; we had a Greek monitor, I think his name was Dimitrios Dagos, and then we had the Busovaca Joint Commission, the members of the Busovaca Joint Commission. The commission was chaired by a Danish monitor, the late A.K.H. Petersen [phoen]. And we had at that time, I think, a German monitor, Dieter Schellschmidt, was a member of the commission. He was a member of the commission. I can't remember what time, but he was a member Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the commission. And then we have different team, monitor teams directly connected to the regional centre, and among those were a Canadian monitor, Remi Landry; and there was later a Greek monitor called Stovos Kinigopoulos; there were a Danish monitor called Allan Laustsen; and later on we had a new monitor in late June, Sir Martin Garrod; and in between we had a Greek monitor, and I can't recall his name. We had during my period as well a Swedish monitor called Torbjorn Junhov; we had a Dutch monitor, Henk Morsink. And we had another Danish monitor. His name was Bent. I can't recall his last name. I think it was Faerge. And that's all I can remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major, for this comprehensive overview. And can you please describe in detail the geographical area of responsibility of the regional centre in Zenica. What -- which municipalities were covered by the regional centre?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was in the west we have Travnik, and followed down to Novi Travnik, Bugojno area. I can't remember if Tomislavgrad was a part of our regional centre, but we had Kiseljak, Visoko, Kakanj, Maglaj, Zavidovici, Zepce, that area. And of course Zenica, where we had our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well, Major. How would you -- how would you, sir, describe the military situation whilst you were deployed in Zenica, the military situation in particular in relation to the HVO-ABiH conflict.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: In the first half of my -- my period in the mission, I saw that HVO were the biggest part. I saw that HVO were the aggressor in the area, and we were able to see that during all the conflicts we witnessed in the Lasva Valley. Later on the Army of BiH succeeded to -- to fight back, and I will not call them "the aggressor" but they were able to conquer some of the lost area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If you are making reference to the Army of BiH within the area you just described, do you make reference to the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- it was the 3rd Corps that -- they were in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say following up your statement you just make -- made that from about mid-May 1993 the ABiH 3rd Corps was more on the attacking side, rather than on the defending side?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can't remember the -- the exact date, but the conflict escalated during the time where we had a -- a Croat massacre against the Ahmici, and after that period the BiH succeeded to -- to pay back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: "Pay back" means they fought back?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. Whilst you've been a member of the ECMM regional centre in Zenica, Major, do you know who was the commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Corps was General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And whilst you were deployed in Zenica, did you have an opportunity to meet General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. I met the general maybe five, six, up to ten times during my -- those three months. Not much in the beginning, because while I was a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission, the deputy or the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Merdan, was normally the -- our contact to the corps. But later on when I was assigned to the area of responsibility in the Zepce, Zavidovici, Maglaj area, I often had to go to the 3rd Corps Command to claim that we were not allowed to pass a checkpoint, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this mean that you had from about mid-May till end of June about ten times the opportunity to meet Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I think ten times is the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Where did General Hadzihasanovic at the time have his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, all the times I had to -- to see the general it was at his office, at his headquarters, close to the steel factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did the meetings, between six to ten meetings, did they take place in General Hadzihasanovic's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did the meetings take place in his office?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, most of them. It was only short meetings, five, ten minutes normal, because we need to have things clarified. But normally at his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please provide us with some information about his office. How did it look like?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can't remember his office like that, but I think -- I can remember that we have to pass the office of his secretary before we came to his office, and in his office there was the normal things you can expect in an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that his office was the normal office for a commander in his position, for a corps commander?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: He was only corps commander in -- in the Bosnian army, so -- I have met, so I don't know what the standard were, but I think the equipment there was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was sufficient to exercise his duties as a corps commander?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can't remember that I saw any radio equipment at his office, but there was a normal telephone and things like that, so I think when he to -- to command his troops, I don't think he was able to do that from his office but maybe at a command post somewhere at the -- the headquarters, but I have only seen his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what was the purpose of your repeated meetings with Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Normally when we have to go to this high level, it was because during our missions in our area of responsibility if we were denied access to a checkpoint, we have to make a complaint. And normally we went directly to -- to the general or to his Chief of Staff, if he was there, trying to solve that, because ECMM had freedom of movement and of course we have to complain every time we were denied this freedom of movement. And there was specific one place -- I can't remember the name of the checkpoint, but several times we were denied access to this checkpoint, and of course we have to make complaints on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After having met General Hadzihasanovic for a number of times, Major, what was your impression in respect to the competence of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It seems to me, with my background at that time, that General Hadzihasanovic was a very competent officer, and he seems that he had an overview over the situation, and he seems to have the ability to command his units. In comparison [Realtime transcript read in error "cooperation"] to the opposite part, General -- then the Colonel Blaskic, there was a big difference on those two commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please a bit elaborate what the difference between these two commanders was about.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Normally when we had meetings with General Hadzihasanovic, he seems very calm and had this overview over the situation; where when you have meetings with the very young Colonel Blaskic, he was more -- he was not calm. He was very stressed and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see my learned friend on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Again, there is a mistake in -- on line 14, "In cooperation to the opposite part." And I believe that the word mentioned by the witness was "comparison with the opposing party."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Was that a comparison or what was it that you said, sir? Can you please look at line 14 in English. It says "in cooperation with." Was it "in cooperation with" or was it "in comparison with"? What was it that you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said "compared to." If you were going to compare those two officers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just saying, Major, that the very young Colonel Blaskic was not calm, he was very stressed, and things like that. And in comparison, you described General Hadzihasanovic as seeming to be very calm and having his overview or an overview over the situation.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct. And I think that because the general has more experience than his -- the opposite part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You had a number of colleagues, Major, within the regional centre of ECMM in Zenica. Did other monitors, ECMM monitors in Zenica, also have meetings or contact with Hadzihasanovic at the time you've been in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. We all had meetings, and some of course had meetings with General Hadzihasanovic as well. I can remember once that one of my Canadian colleagues were -- Remi Landry was maybe that colleague that had the best knowledge of the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how did it become apparent to you that your colleague Remi Landry had the best knowledge of General Hadzihasanovic? Why?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can remember that they went fishing once, and I think that during his -- Remi Landry's tour on the mission that he was the most experienced monitor we had and he was very often having meetings at the 3rd Corps Command. So I think that therefore he had relations on a -- a professional level with -- with the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This relation, was it closer than anybody else's relation within ECMM, the relation between Remi Landry and General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: He was the only one that went out fishing with the general. I don't know how my other colleagues, if they had any social contact with the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: They went fishing. Major, can you please assist me. How was it possible that General Hadzihasanovic, who was fighting a war on two front lines, how was it possible that he had the time to go fishing between April and June 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Sometimes - and I know that myself - as a commander, you need to relax, and if there are a break in the fighting, then you have to do something else. And I can imagine that that's one of the reasons. And if you are a commander and you have a good deputy or Chief of Staff, then he can take over for a short period. So I see nothing in this that he went out fishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying that a commander needs to relax if there are a break in the fighting. During the time period you've been in Zenica, were there such breaks in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The time period were very tense, but sometimes the tension were higher than other days so there were a few days with -- where it was calm, without big incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, did you also get in contact with General Hadzihasanovic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I very often had the opportunity to have meetings with General Merdan; that was the deputy or Chief of Staff of the 3rd Corps. He was a high-ranking member of -- from BiH in the Busovaca Joint Commission. And later on he was a member of the joint command in Travnik, and later on I was working together with him in the -- in the investigation of a kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Before we address the issues of -- related to the various kidnappings, how close after you had a number of meetings with Mr. Merdan and Mr. Hadzihasanovic, how close were the two?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I think they were working very close, and I -- I recognised Merdan as a very loyal officer to General Hadzihasanovic, and every time when we asked Merdan for something and asked him to bring something to the general, we very often have an answer later the same day or maybe next day. But -- so I think they have very good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, you already touched on the issues of kidnappings. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when and how you did become aware of kidnappings.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We had a contact from Colonel Blaskic, the commander of the HVO of regional zone Central Bosnia, and he told our headquarters that four of his staff officers were kidnapped close to the front in the -- the Travnik area. And he asked ECMM to investigate in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And when did you receive the information about this kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was in -- I can't remember the exact date, but it was in -- in the beginning of April, within the first week or maybe the second week in April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In addition to this incident of kidnapping, did you become aware of another or another incidents of kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, there was in total three kidnappings. There was another kidnapping later on where the HVO brigade commander - I think his name was Totic - were kidnapped in Zenica. This brigade commander was ambushed together with his four bodyguards and the four bodyguards were killed and an eyewitness to the situation was killed as well, and the brigade commander was taken out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, now, you have described two kidnappings. You were saying that there were in total three kidnappings. Can you please inform us about the third kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The third kidnapping that took place in -- in this period was from the local radio station. I think it was called Radio CD. It was a radio station, and as far as I can remember it was founded by the Americans. And there were two or three persons from that radio station, two journalists or technicians - I can't remember what their job were there - they were kidnapped as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, did you receive official information in your capacity as an ECMM monitor as to who was responsible for the kidnappings you just described?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No, not in the beginning. In the beginning, General Blaskic asked ECMM to head the investigation in this kidnapping, and a team were -- with the Spanish monitor Juan Valentin and I, together with Mr. Merdan, and the deputy or the Chief of Staff of the HVO, Franjo Nakic, was a member of this small investigation team. And in the beginning, we have -- we didn't know where to start, but Colonel Blaskic, from HVO, claimed that it was the 7th Muslim Brigade that was responsible for this kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How did it come that General Hadzihasanovic's deputy, Merdan, was involved in this team investigating the kidnapping -- the kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I don't know why it was Mr. Merdan, but I think that my headquarters has decided that when we were going to do those investigations, it was necessary to have a high-ranking officer from -- from HVO and a high-ranking officer from BiH. So both the two deputies from the two corps levels were present in the investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When you started the investigation, together with Mr. Merdan and a representative of the HVO, what were the allegations, suspicions about who was responsible for the kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic said that it was the 7th Muslim Brigade that was responsible for this. That was -- normally, every time there was some incident that the BiH have done something, the normal unit that was -- that the HVO claims that were behind this normally was the 7th Muslim Brigade. But in this specific area where the four officers were kidnapped, I think it was the area of responsibility of the 4th Muslim Brigade -- sorry, the 7th Muslim Brigade, though it could -- it could be the 7th Muslim Brigade that was behind the kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were doing the investigation, not only in respect to the four kidnapped HVO officers but also in respect to the kidnapping of Commander Totic, did there come a time when you received information from the kidnappers?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. After I used several days trying to see if we could find the kidnapped officers, certainly two messengers from what we called Mujahedins arrived to our headquarters with a letter claiming that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mujahedins, or as they called themselves, the Arabic Group, that they were responsible for the kidnapping and they had the four officers. And I can't remember if they mentioned Totic in the same letter, but they said that they had the kidnapped persons and they want to have some of their Muslim brothers who was in the custody of HVO released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The two messengers from what you called Mujahedins or the Arabic Group, were they actually foreigners? Were they Arabs?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: They were dressed in Arabic clothes, in this robe, and they -- as far as -- I cannot remember if they were having an Arabic look, but I think as normally when we discussed this we said it was Arabic persons who -- who came with the letters. I can't remember it myself, but I can remember from our discussions that it was people from -- not Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you still recall what was written in the letter? Have you seen the letter yourself?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the letter -- or there were two letters, one in English and one in -- in German. And the text in the two letters was identical. I can remember that it was dated with the -- the Muslim date. It was not April 1993 but another date. And there was a lot of praise to Allah in it. They keep ECMM responsible for the exchange of prisoners. And if this exchange wouldn't take place, we would be responsible for the killing of the -- the hostages. And I can remember the letter was signed with some Arabic signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I would like to show the witness the letter, which is number 16 on the Prosecution's contested exhibit list, and the letter will also appear via Sanction on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, if you could please have a look at the handwritten letter. Is this the letter you were just talking about, the letter you received from the Mujahedin, them claiming being responsible for the kidnappings and them asking you to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But as far as I can remember, there was a German version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you received the very same letter in both the English language and the German language?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is the letter you have in front of you, is it the letter in the English language?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. This is the English version of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were the English version and the German version of the letter, were they identical?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, because we compared the two letters to see if there were any difference in -- in the context, but there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was somebody with you at ECMM in Zenica who spoke German, or was it a German national?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We had a German monitor, Dieter Schellschmidt, who was of course able to speak German. Then we were a few other persons who was able to speak German as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution wishes to tender this handwritten letter into evidence. So far it has been a contested document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What has the Defence to tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any objections, Your Honour. This document -- handwritten document may be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, do you have anything to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, given what the witness has now testified to, we have no objection to this document being admitted into evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be P109.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the time you were -- or ECMM in Zenica was dealing with the issue of the kidnapped HVO officers, how often did the Mujahedin come to ECMM?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number of times where we had a visit from -- from the Arabic Group or the Mujahedins, because I was not participating in those meetings. But they were there several times. A small -- a body was created to solve this problem and to do the negotiations, and among those participants were of course ECMM; as far as I can remember, the International Committee of the Red Cross were participating; HVO were participating. I can't remember exactly if there were any participations from BiH, but as far as I can remember they were invited to participate, and during those negotiations the International Red Cross wanted the permission to visit the hostages but this was denied from the Mujahedins, but it was agreed to let the hostages send letters and I think a videotape to their family and to their -- their commanders so they were able to see that they were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The repeated meetings you were just talking about, did they take place in the Hotel Internacional in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, it took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how did the Mujahedin come to the Hotel Internacional in Zenica? Did they use a car, or did they come by feet?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can remember when the first messengers arrived, they were arriving in a car, and I can remember that we later on saw or recognised the same car another place. How they came to meetings other times, I don't know, because I was not always present when they were there, but I can remember in the beginning normally they were armed, and we didn't want to have armed soldiers or mercenaries in our compound. But unfortunately, the BiH civilian policeman who was trying to secure our headquarters, he always disappeared when the Mujahedins arrived. So sometimes they had weapons inside and other times they showed up without arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did they actually have?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Normally they were wearing AK-47s, the Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Obviously an automatic rifle, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's discuss this issue with the car they used at the beginning negotiating about the release of the Mujahedin hostages. I understand the Mujahedin for the first time arrived at the Hotel Internacional, the regional centre Zenica of ECMM, at about mid-April, second half of April 1993? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. It was -- there was a lot of days after we started the investigations -- I can't remember how much, maybe ten days after we started the investigations we had this first contact from Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And you were just saying a few minutes ago that, "We later on saw or recognised the same car at another place." Can you please inform the Trial Chamber where and, if you recall, as to when you have seen or recognised the very same car.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can remember that it was discussed later on because the same car that was used by the two Mujahedins were later on observed at one of the 7 Muslim Brigade's -- unit's headquarters. I can't recall if it was at the headquarters or their compound at the music school in Zenica or it was in the Ravno Rostovo, but one of those two places this vehicle was observed in front of the -- the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please provide us some more detail, if you do recall, as to when the very same car the Mujahedin used to come to the regional centre of ECMM in Zenica to negotiate about the release of the Mujahedin prisoners and the HVO hostages, do you recall as to when this issue that the very same car was seen in front of the 7th Muslim Brigade headquarter or command, do you recall when roughly?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but I can -- can remember that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discussed the matter because we were looking to see if we can find a link between the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedins. HVO claimed that Mujahedin was a part of 7th Muslim Brigade, but we didn't see any link. The only link we saw was that this car has been observed in front of one of their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it prior to the release of the hostages? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it during the time you yourself have been in Zenica, meaning between April and end of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what efforts, if any, have been made by ECMM to get the hostage problem resolved, and if so, how was it actually resolved.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: After a lot of negotiations, we succeeded to -- to solve the problem in -- in May. At that time, I think the situation had covered a period of a month or more. And it was agreed -- as I said earlier, I was not a member of this working group but I took part in the work while we were going to release the hostages. And Arab group and HVO agreed to release -- from the Arab group side, they released the four HVO staff officers and the brigade commander, as well I think that kidnapped journalist was released as well. But it was agreed that this release should take place at three different places, where I was responsible for the release in Travnik, where the four HVO officers should be released by the Mujahedin. A Dutch colleague, Henk Morsink, I think, was possible to the release of -- at a factory, a Mediapan factory or something like that. There was a factory between Vitez and Zenica, in that area. And he was responsible for release there. And then there should be a release in Zenica, where all the foreigners, all the Arabic members of Mujahedin, should be released. And all those released should be coordinated. It had to take time -- at the same time, all three places. And while I was in Travnik, I was there together with an armed escort from the British Battalion in Vitez, and I was there accompanied by a Mujahedin who was able to speak German, so I was able to communicate with him. The whole operation were delayed several times, I think. It was planned that the release should take place at 12.00, but it was delayed several times. I think the release took place in the -- in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were in Travnik, I understand. Who was the responsible ECMM member who was responsible for the operation in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I think that my German colleague, Dieter Schellschmidt, was one of the persons who was responsible for the whole operation. And as far as I can remember, he was dealing with the matter in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who from the HVO side, Major, who was exchanged for the Mujahedin, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Who was released from ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whom did the Mujahedin release?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. They released the four -- in Travnik, the four officers, and I can't remember where Totic was released, if he was released in Zenica or in -- in the other place at the Mediapan factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What did you get to know, Major, about the release that took place in Zenica and all the aspects surrounding this release?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Because I was in Travnik, I was not able to -- to monitor it myself, but later on my German colleague, Dieter Schellschmidt, told me about the situation in Zenica. He told me that a lot of Mujahedins were -- came to the area in front of the hotel, and he told me that the local police disappeared when the armed Mujahedins arrived. He told me that there was a truck with a heavy machine-gun mounted on the truck as well, and he told me that after the HVO had released all the -- the detained persons, the detained persons together with the Mujahedins left the area and there was a lot of happy shooting in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know, Major, whether ECMM monitor Schellschmidt, your colleague at the regional centre in Zenica, whether he wrote a report about the operation in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, he did, because after this operation was finished, he made a report where he had this chronology on -- with time scheduled for the different incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you get a chance to read the report at the time in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to see the report and I had the opportunity to have a copy of that report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, I would like to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit P155, which is the ECMM regional centre Zenica report of 19th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please have a look at the report, and please take your time. Is this the report of Dieter Schellschmidt you were just testifying about?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The English version, the translated version, is not made by ECMM, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may, please, draw your attention, Major, at paragraph 4 on the first page, the second half of paragraph 4 reads as follows: "The exchange was achieved only due to the very close cooperation between all parties involved. These were: ICRC, UNPROFOR, HVO, ABiH; the Arabian Group (Mujahedin) and ECMM as mediator. Representatives of all these organisations were present at all three places during the exchange." Is what is written in this report, to your knowledge is it correct? Has Mr. Schellschmidt correctly reflected in his report what took place?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As I didn't participate in all the meetings, I'm not the one to tell if -- who was participating at the different meetings, but at the place in Travnik where I was responsible for -- for the release, I cannot remember that there were other -- that HVO or BiH or ICRC were present. As far as I can remember, it was only UNPROFOR who was providing us with this armed escort and the representative from the Mujahedin who was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you have any reason, Major, to disbelieve what is written in Mr. Schellschmidt's report?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No. And because all our -- our reports made by ECMM is countersigned. Normally our team reports have been signed by both the two monitors, and that's the same with other reports, that our people who are able to confirm the context in the -- in the document. But as I didn't participate in those meetings, I'm not able to say who participated in the -- in the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That, I do understand, Major. If I may draw your attention to paragraph 6 on the first page. And you already testified about this particular aspect. It reads: "At Zenica in front of the Hotel Internacional the Mujahedins showed up with a force of at least 100 masked and heavily armed soldiers (probably members of the 7th Muslim Brigade)." The last sentence in brackets. In your discussions, if any, with Mr. Schellschmidt, was this issue discussed or reported?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can remember that we discussed that there was a lot of heavily armed soldiers in -- in front of the hotel. I cannot remember the discussion, if it was only members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. As far as I can remember the discussion, there was members from the Mujahedins there as well. But sometimes it could be very difficult to see the difference, because sometimes members of the 7th Muslim Brigade were wearing the same type of clothes as we normally observed the Mujahedins wearing, and other times some Mujahedins were wearing uniform, so it could be difficult to see if this was a member of 7th Muslim Brigade or he was a member of the Mujahedins. Very often you had to see it on his -- maybe his face or to listen to his mother tongue, to listen to his -- to his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may, Major, if I may draw your attention to Annex B, which is page 3 of the document compilation. And if I may draw your attention specifically to paragraph 6, where it says: "RC Zenica informed immediately HQ/ECMM, 3rd Corps ABiH and BiH civilian police," and a number Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of other organisations. Do you have any reason to disbelieve that this statement in the report is not correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If you may, please, sir, have a look at paragraph 10 of the Annex B, the second in which it says: "The Mujahedin were also informed by RC about the HVO proposal. This time they replied that they wanted a meeting with HVO 3rd Corps ABiH, 7th Muslim Brigade, ECMM, ICRC," and a number of further organisations, "to discuss the exchange and the whole problem concerning the foreigners."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see my learned friend on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would like to give my colleague all the necessary leeway in order for him to ask questions that concern hearsay information he may have obtained from others. This is a matter that has been discussed before the Trial Chamber on a number of occasions. We know that hearsay is a form of evidence that can be accepted under certain circumstances; nevertheless, it's necessary to check the reliability of the source and it's also necessary to determine whether the source is available and could appear here to testify. In this case, the author of the document is a witness who will be heard by the Trial Chamber, so I don't see why one should ask this witness whether he believes his colleague or not, given that the colleague will be appearing here and will be able to tell us about the facts. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you have heard the comment made by the Defence. According to the Defence, you will be able to ask the author of this document these questions, so is it really necessary to ask this officer to confirm what is contained in this document, given that the author of this document can confirm its contents? But you certainly have a good reason for asking this question. Could you respond to the objection raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the Prosecution has a good reason to ask this witness. We actually have a number of reasons. Number one, the report is a summary in respect to the number of prisoner exchanges. And Mr. Schellschmidt has wrote a summary in respect to issues he was himself involved in and, in addition, in respect to facts and issues others, like the witness today, was involved in. The witness today already informed the Trial Chamber that he was to some extent involved in the issue of receiving letters from the Mujahedin; he has participated in the exchange of hostages held by the Mujahedin. So this witness is certainly, in addition to the author of the report, in a position to comment on whatever is written in the report. Number two, the Prosecution is of the view if a witness who is not the author of the report corroborates what is written in the report, corroborates it to the extent possible - and I do appreciate the comment made by my learned friends from the Defence that in some respects he can only -- only testify about what he had heard from Mr. Schellschmidt - however, the Prosecution is of the view that corroborated evidence by a number of different witnesses strengthens the evidence that Mr. Schellschmidt may give at a later point in time during these proceedings, and therefore the Prosecution would like to continue to ask this witness questions in relation to that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will give the floor to Mr. Bourgon again. But in order to summarise the Prosecution's position, according to the Prosecution there is a report drafted by a witness who will be appearing in the future, but given that this witness himself participated in the matter of prisoner exchange, the witness can naturally answer questions concerning the exchange. In addition, he could provide additional support for the contents of the report drafted by the witness who will be appearing in the future. Mr. Bourgon, before we have our break, what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Regard to the first issue, yes, the witness did participate in this exchange and he can give an account of the facts. He can tell us about what he heard, what he saw, but he cannot say whether he believes his colleague. As far as the second issue is concerned, corroboration means to add something in order to support it. But to ask the witness whether he believes the contents of the report or not doesn't allow us to support the main claim. If the witness says, "I saw such and such an act committed by such and such a person" - and this is something that is contained in the document - that would constitute a corroboration. But asking him whether he believes that what is contained in the document or not is not a corroboration. This is just a matter of seeing whether the author, Mr. Schellschmidt, is credible or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume after the break. It is now quarter to 4.00. We will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We resume the session. The Chamber has posed a question regarding the objection put forth by Mr. Bourgon. The Chamber has taken into account the importance of the document. The Prosecution may ask -- put all the questions to this witness with regard to the importance of this witness. So, Mr. Withopf, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, if I may come back to this document in front of you, and this is actually the last issue I wanted to address in the context of this document. Prior to the break, I drew your attention already to paragraph 10 of Annex B, where it reads: "This time they replied that they wanted a meeting with HVO 3rd Corps ABiH, 7th Muslim Brigade, ECMM, ICRC and UNPROFOR to discuss the exchange and the whole problem concerning the foreigners." Major, do you have any reason to disbelieve what's written here under paragraph 10?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the exhibit please be removed from the witness. Mr. President, Your Honours, there are three further issues I wish to address, and for you and Defence counsel's information, I anticipate it will take me no longer than 20 to 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, you already earlier on mentioned that you got to know about the Zenica Music School. To your knowledge, sir, which military unit was based in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: At the music school in Zenica, there was a sort of a unit headquarters from the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What does it mean, "A sort of a unit headquarters from the 7th Muslim Brigade"? If you could please elaborate a bit on this.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember if it was actually the brigade headquarters or maybe a battalion headquarters or something, but it was a sort of a headquarter but I cannot remember the level of this headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What did you get to know, sir -- what did you get to know about the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to -- to meet the brigade several times, the first time during the investigation in this kidnapping incident; and later on, where I was chairing this joint humanitarian commission, where I had access to the music school, I had the opportunity to -- to meet soldiers from that unit again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may please follow up. Where, at what places, in what areas did you meet members of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: At first, during the -- the investigation in the kidnapping case we had this meeting at the hotel in -- I'm not sure that I'm pronouncing it correctly, in Ravno Rostovo, in this former ski hotel or ski motel, where we had a meeting with the local commander. And when I say "the local commander," everyone introduced themselves as a commander at that time, so it's very difficult to -- to say if it was a battalion commander or the brigade commander. But I cannot recall the name of the person, but the person who was the highest rank and the commander, when we visited that day, he showed us the compound. And after we have -- or Mr. Merdan told him why we came, and that we would like to see the motel, to see if the hostages was at that spot, and they were very polite to us, and the commander showed us around and we were able to see the whole compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Major, was it Merdan, the ABiH 3rd Corps deputy commander, who suggested to go to this place which I think - and you may please confirm it - is called Ravno Rostovo? Was it Merdan who suggested to go to this place where the 7th Muslim Brigade had some sort of a headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And this visit to Ravno Rostovo, was it in the context of investigating the kidnapping of HVO officers by Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: At that time, we didn't knew that it was Mujahedin that was behind this kidnapping. We only heard the rumours from Colonel Blaskic that it could be the 7th Muslim Brigade who was responsible. That's the reason for us to go to this headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In what area -- in which area, Major, is this village Ravno Rostovo located? What's the closest town?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As I can remember the geography, it was south-west of Novi Travnik, close to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you notice at this 7th Muslim Brigade headquarters in Ravno Rostovo close to Bugojno, did you notice any military flags or insignia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: At first, when we arrived to the place, there were soldiers outside that welcomed us with some -- they were yelling something that included Allah's name. It was maybe in Arabic. And they were having a lot of green banners with some Arabic signs on it, to include a flag, a green flag with some Arabic signs on it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's briefly address -- or let's address your visit to the Zenica Music School. Do you recall, even if it's roughly only, as to when you visited the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: My visit to the music school was not during the investigation of the hostages but was when I was chairing this joint humanitarian commission. We heard rumours that there should be deterred persons at the music school, and at that time, before we started to release prisoners -- or not prisoners but detained persons, we would like to visit all the spots where we have heard there were people or there were even only rumours that there should be people. That's the reason for us to go to -- to the music school. And normally we did not have access to the music school, but because I was chairing this commission, I had a signed letter. I can't remember who signed it, but it was signed above corps level, so I think it was on general staff level, the commanding generals, they had signed this letter. And this letter should give me access to all places in the Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who was with you when you visited the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: When we visit the music school, the rest of the commission, the joint humanitarian commission, were present. But as far as I can remember, I was the only one who had access to go inside to see the music school. At first we were denied access to the music school, and I have to have a contact to the 3rd Corps, and as far as I can remember, I had a contact to Mr. Merdan and he mediated, so we were able -- or I was able to come into the music school. The local representatives from -- from the 7th Muslim Brigade didn't want members from HVO to come into this music school, and to try to -- to solve the problems, we agreed that I went in without the rest of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who did deny you access to the music school?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It was the man who was the commander -- the man who was responsible for the compound or for the unit that was at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long, Major, had you to wait before you got approval by Merdan, the ABiH 3rd Corps deputy commander, to have access to the music school?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think I had to wait for one hour or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To wait to get access to a certain premises, was it a usual experience you made, in respect to 3rd Corps premises?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Normally we did not have any problems with getting access to -- to units or to compounds belonging to Armija BiH. On the opposite side, we had very often problems with HVO, but normally we did not have problems with BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: So in respect to premises or detention facilities ran by ABiH 3rd Corps units, would it be fair to say that this was an exceptional, if not even a very exceptional, situation?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. Because normally we had direct access to go to the compound, but this time we were not -- we were denied access in the beginning, but later on, after this one hour, we had access.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may please come back to my starting question: Do you recall as to when you visited the Zenica Music School, if it's only roughly?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: This joint humanitarian commission started the work, I think it was the 10th of June, 1993, so it has been just after that, maybe the 11th or the 12th perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you actually see any detainees in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No. I was allowed to see the whole music school. There was only one exception, and that was a room where they claimed that it was their signal room. And normally I went -- we were visiting headquarters that didn't want us to see what type of signal equipment they had. I could see that through the door into this room there was running some cables, some antenna cables, maybe some power supply cables, so I was not that suspicious when they said, "Okay, we don't want you to go in here because it is our signal room." That was very normal when we were visiting headquarters. And we were very often accused to be spies, and we don't want to -- to show up being spying at the headquarters, so we agreed not to see that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it a normal -- a usual experience, Major, that both warring factions in Central Bosnia, namely, the HVO and the ABiH 3rd Corps, tried to hide their communication equipment and communication abilities?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was normal, as is normal for every army, to try to -- to hide this equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, you have been provided access to, in your view, to all rooms in the Zenica Music School but the room which you describe as a communications room?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. They told us it was their communications room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P8. And it will also appear on the front of you, Major, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Major, have you ever seen to your recollection this room which is displayed on the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It seems to be a basement, but I cannot recall to have seen this specific location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the exhibit please be removed from the witness. For the record, for the transcript, witness Lars Baggesen was shown Prosecution Exhibit P8, a photograph which displays the basement of the Zenica Music School, and the witness was stating that he can't recall having seen this room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long, Major, have you been in the Zenica Music School at that day in the second half of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember how long a time I was there, but I was shown around at the school and I was able after my visits at the school to make a drawing, because I was the first to our knowledge that have been at the school, so we didn't have any sketch showing the school. And concerning the -- the basement, we knew there was this basement, and I mentioned that there was one room we didn't have access to. That was the -- the communications room. And I think that if we haven't been allowed to see the basement, I would have been suspicious, but I was not able to recall the picture. I remember to say, "Okay, this room was the basement."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When you visited the Zenica Music School in June 1993, did you notice any foreigners in the Zenica Music School, any Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: During our visits, there were soldiers in uniform and there were soldiers in -- in Arabic clothes. We didn't have the opportunity to speak with all the persons there. But I think that some of the persons there could have been not -- non-Bosniaks, but it could be difficult to -- to see and make the conclusion that it was an Arabic man if we hadn't been speaking with him and, as I said earlier on, sometimes we were able to see that he has an Arabic face or something like that, but I cannot -- I can only recall that there were soldiers in uniform and there were soldiers in these clothes as Arabic Group or the Mujahedin normally were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next issue, Major, and it will be very briefly addressed, the communication abilities. You already testified that both parties to the conflict, namely, the HVO and the ABiH 3rd Corps, tried to hide their communication equipment and the communication abilities to the international observers. Two very brief questions: To your knowledge, at the time you've been in Zenica who was in control of the PTT building in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I don't know if it was the 3rd Corps who was in control of the PTT building, but it was under the control of the Muslim inhabitants there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the second issue I wish to address in this context: Did you ever get to know whether the ABiH 3rd Corps used a mobile communications system?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We knew that they were using other types of communications systems, because sometimes they were able to communicate in areas where we knew that the normal land line were cut down. We saw not directly mobile telephones, but later on I have learnt that they were in possession of sophisticated communication systems, but I didn't see it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on, Major, to the very last issue I wish to address; that's the ABiH detention facility in Mehurici. Sir, did there come a time when you visited the ABiH 3rd Corps detention facility in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. I visited this facility at the -- at the school during the work with the joint humanitarian commission, and our findings were that a lot of civilians were detained at the school, more than 200 civilians were detained. Most of them were women and children, even babies, and there was a few elderly people amongst them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just mentioning, sir, that the about or more than 200 civilians, including women, children, and babies were detained in a school. In what area, to your knowledge of the school, were they detained?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: They were detained in the gymnasium or in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the purpose of you visiting the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: During the work in the joint humanitarian commission, we had to visit all places where we knew or where we had heard rumours that there should be detained persons on the HVO side and on the BiH side. That's the reason for us to go to -- to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And have you been involved in negotiations about the release of the civilians detained in the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. After we had overall view over the detained persons on both sides, we started the negotiations to release all the detained persons. And it was agreed in the commission that we should have this overview before we started to release prisoners -- not prisoners, detained persons. And it was agreed that it should be all-for-all release but on different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Parties of the commission you are referring to were the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And which party made the decision in respect to the release of the civilian detainees in the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: This was, of course, discussed with the two BiH members in -- in the commission, and they of course had the mandate from the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I'll now give the floor to Defence counsel. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Bagessen. We've had the pleasure of meeting this morning, along with my colleague Rodney Dixon representing the accused Amir Kubura. But for the record, let me introduce myself once again. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and this afternoon I am accompanied with Mrs. Edina Residovic and Mr. Alexis Demirdjian, and together we represent the accused General Hadzihasanovic, who as you know, was the commander of the 3rd Corps in Central Bosnia. Major Bagessen, I would like to begin by asking you a few general questions before moving on into more specific issues, such as, of course, those that you have discussed with the Prosecution; namely, the kidnappings, the exchange, and a couple of other issues, visits to the music school and to Mehurici. Before that, I would like to confirm, Major, that you testified in the Blaskic case and in the Kordic case as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the basis for both of these appearances was a statement which you provided to investigators of the Prosecution in 1996. I guess it was in the month of August. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I recall it was in 1996, but not the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then you were again contacted by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and you provided a further statement in February of 2001, which was dealing more specifically with this case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you went to Bosnia, you actually spent three months in Central Bosnia, and that was from the end of March till the 1st day of July.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the time, you were a captain in the Danish Army, but if I recall correctly, you were 36 years old, which is a bit older than the average captain. Can you explain if there's a reason for this, in terms of your military background.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, that's a normal age for a captain in the Danish Army, and actually I was promoted to major at 38, and that was a young major at that time in the Danish Army, so there's nothing in the age.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
