utterances.text: So but at 36 years old, did you feel you had more experience than other captains, for example, from other -- from BritBat, than you may have encountered during your stay in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, at that time, in the Danish Army you had to be captain for ten years before you can get -- be promoted to major. So I was -- as a captain, I was experienced, an experienced captain. Compared to captains from other countries, I don't know. I'm not able to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major. Moving on to -- during your time in Bosnia, you served, of course, with the ECMM, and you were attached to the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be correct in stating the mission of the ECMM in Central Bosnia as being to assist in maintaining peace and stability and preventing the occurrence of possible conflict within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if a conflict nevertheless occurs, which is actually the case, the Monitoring Mission will assist in establishing the facts to avoid further deterioration of the situation? Would that be a fair statement of your understanding of the ECMM mission?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that may be more correct than the answer I gave earlier this day, but I could not remember all the -- the fine words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's perfectly understandable, Major, because I took it from a document, which I would like to show you at this time, which is the creation of the ECMM mission in -- for Bosnia and Herzegovina. And we have enough copies to show everyone, in terms of what was the mandate or the mission of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a number of documents that we would like to tender into evidence. We don't have them in the accused's language. Nevertheless, we have discussed these documents. We've discussed them with the accused. But our lack of resources means that we're not in the position to translate all the documents that were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... where it says "mandate" and simply confirm that what I just read to you is actually the mandate of the European Community Monitoring Mission that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, I will say that again. Can you simply look at Article 1, on the first page, and confirm that this refers to the mission, the European Community Monitoring Mission, that you were a member of.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's a minor and it's a pure technical issue, and it may only be related to the copy we got, but it appears that, at least in the copy we got, maybe page 1 or even page 2, are missing, since the document starts with: "Together herein after called the participating parties," and one would expect that there's something at the beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as we know, this is a document we obtained during our investigations and the document starts normally. We have an introduction, followed by Articles. There's Article 1, the mandate; Article 2, 3, 4, 5, and it continues up until the end. We're only tendering this document into evidence in order to assist the Chamber in understanding the ECMM mission. If there are any objections, we'll withdraw the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like a document number, because the witness has recognised this document as an ECMM document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, the Defence would like to tender this document into evidence. It's been signed by President Izetbegovic, the ambassador representing the EU, but on the other hand, I don't have the signature of the Federal secretary for foreign affairs in the document that I have, Mr. Budimir Loncar, there is no signature. There must be a reason for this. Apparently there is an introduction in this document, and it also contains 11 Articles. What is the Prosecution's position with regard to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's no objection. However, I wish to emphasise that obviously a part is missing, and that the document is containing handwritten portions. But again, there's no objection of the Prosecution to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll mark the document for identification. If the Defence provides us with a more complete document at a subsequent date --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's the only document -- the only copy we have. I wanted to assist the Chamber. But if you want, we can mark this document for identification or we can withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, given the importance of this document, and if you say that you don't have another copy, we'll admit it. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number for this document will be DH166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm showing you a further document which is basically an organigramme of the organisation of the ECMM. I would like you to take a look at this document and to let me know whether this corresponds to the mission of the EUMM and especially the part with respect to Regional Centre Zenica.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, as I can see, this is a mix through the period, because at the time the joint humanitarian commission was established, the Busovaca Joint Commission did not exist. At the time I was there, the name of the mission was the European Community Monitoring Mission and not the EUMM. But we had the RC Zenica and connected to RC Zenica we had in the beginning the Busovaca Joint Commission. Later on we had the joint humanitarian commission. But they were not established at the same time. While we had the Busovaca Joint Commission we did not have the CC Travnik. The CC Travnik was established later on, but we had the CC Tuzla and we had the CC Mostar. CC, that's coordination centres. And in connection to those coordination centres, we have the teams; namely, Tango 1, Tango 2, Victor 1 to Victor 4, and Mike 1 to Mike 4. And before CC Travnik were established, Victor 1 and Victor 2 was directly placed under the RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major. So would I be right in saying that the -- if I start from the Regional Centre Zenica we could say that the Busovaca Joint Commission was the first to exist and that at some point in time it was replaced by the joint humanitarian commission? We will go through specific dates --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- later on.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: The Busovaca Joint Commission was not replaced by the joint humanitarian commission. The Busovaca Joint Commission was replaced by the joint command in Travnik, and the joint command -- the Busovaca Joint Commission were chaired by ECMM. The joint command in Travnik was a joint command with HVO and BiH, and ECMM was only there as observers to monitor the cooperation there. We were not members like that. The joint humanitarian commission was a specific commission that was established in connection to a cease-fire agreement signed in June -- the 10th of June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness has mentioned a number of amendments, has changed certain things, I don't want to tender the document. But we will introduce the document in three stages. We'll present it through another witness in order to assist the Trial Chamber to obtain a very precise view of the situation as far as the mission is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... that you yourself reported directly to the Regional Centre Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the beginning of your question because you started your question before the translator has finished the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry. You are able to confirm, Major, that you reported yourself directly to the Regional Centre Zenica.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I did that while I was a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission. I did that while I was team leader on the Victor 1 or Victor 2, because at that time they were directly under RC Zenica and later on, when I was chairing the joint humanitarian commission, I reported directly to RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major. If I can go on to the fact that during your three months in Bosnia, am I right in saying that you were away for a period of approximately 10 days in May?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. I had a leave and -- in May, and I can remember I was in Denmark. I think it was the last, end of May I was in Denmark on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is the normal procedure to -- for sending states to have their personnel go back to their own country at least once during their tour?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that most countries at that time would send their people for tours of six months but that your country decided that the tours would be only three months because of the exceptionally difficult circumstances of this particular mission? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It's correct concerning that Denmark was only sending monitors there for a three-month period. I cannot remember how long the other countries, how long a time they were there, but at that time it was three months for Danish monitors. Later on it was extended to -- to six months as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the reason for three months at that time was due to the exceptional character and the difficulty of this particular mission.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is -- am I right in saying, Major, that for you personally this mission was a very difficult mission, both physically but even more so morally, and that for this reason you completed a war diary so that you could simply give your war diary to your friends, rather than have to again and again explain everything, all the horrible things that you had seen?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct that I kept this war diary. It was a private diary I kept so I was able to not make an official report but just to -- during the nights I have to recall some things, to work against to see, because we witnessed a lot of killings and things like that. So to be a whole person, you have to work with things like that. So that's why I kept this diary. And when I came back to Denmark, I rewrite it on my computer word for word from the -- the handwritten and word for word to my computer, and then I gave a copy of this diary to members of my family, friends, and colleagues, so I didn't have to tell the same stories again and again. Because it was very difficult to -- to speak of all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Let me move on to the Busovaca Joint Commission. Are you able to confirm, Major, that this commission was born on the 27th of January at a meeting which was chaired by General Gordy Simpson from UNPROFOR and was attended by Colonel Blaskic from the HVO and Mr. Merdan, from the ABiH? Can you confirm this? Is this something that you know of?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I know that the Busovaca Joint Commission was established before I arrived to theatre, and I know that the agreement was signed in Busovaca and that's why it was named Busovaca Joint Commission. But I don't know who participated in this meeting and who signed that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Now, you are aware that this commission, the Busovaca Joint Commission, was meant to meet daily and to receive the complaints from both sides with respect to any breaking of the cease-fire or any complaints with violations that were happening on both sides?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We had a meeting every morning. As I recall, it was 7.00 or 8.00. We had a meeting in a house that ECMM has rented in Vitez. And we had a meeting, of course chaired by ECMM and with representatives from HVO and BiH. Mr. Merdan was the senior representative from BiH, and Franjo Nakic was the senior representative from HVO. And every morning we started to look at the incidents that had happened the last 24 hours, and after that we had a small discussion, and then we split up in some teams, and those teams consist of one monitor, one interpreter, one member of the HVO, one member of BiH. And then we went to spots to do some fact-finding. Very often we used time to do fact-finding on rumours, and I realised that the first victim in a conflict is truth. So very often we went out to do fact-finding, so it was only a rumour. There have been no killings, there have been no looting, there was no burnt houses. But other times we realised that it was not a rumour, it was correct, there have been lootings, there have been snipering in that area, there have been inhabitants killed or similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And am I right in saying, Major, that the Busovaca Joint Commission reported to a Busovaca Joint Commission coordinating committee, which sat approximately biweekly at a higher level and that this committee would have in attendance people like General Morillon, General Petkovic, General Halilovic, Ambassador Thebault from, of course, your own ECMM, and Colonel Stewart, who was the commander of the BritBat?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It's correct. Colonel Stewart was commander of the BritBat at that -- in the beginning of the period I was in the Busovaca Joint Commission. He was replaced later on. The Busovaca Joint Commission -- the ECMM part of the Busovaca Joint Commission, we reported to the Regional Centre Zenica, and then Regional Centre Zenica, I think, reported further up in the system. But our report from the Busovaca Joint Commission went directly to the RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But are you able to confirm, Major, the existence of this coordination committee at the higher level?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall that there were a commission like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we move on to the death of the Busovaca Joint Commission, if I may use this expression, can you confirm that this happened in April and -- because of the incidents, the most important of which would be the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember the reason for the so-called death of the Busovaca Joint Commission. As I remember it, we saw the new joint headquarters as a step in the right direction, because it was a step further than this commission chaired by ECMM. But it was a new body where the two parts were able to coordinate the work for -- for peace in the area. But -- and it's correct, it was after the -- the massacre in Ahmici. But I cannot recall if that was the reason to make the new joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if I suggest to you, Major, that the -- in relation to Ahmici or the events at that specific time in April, the fact that hostilities opened again between the two parties, that was the end of the commission because you can no longer cooperate. The parties could no longer cooperate with one another.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I'm a little in doubt about -- about the dates. I can't remember the dates when the Busovaca Joint Commission was closed down and the new -- the new joint command was established. I can't remember the exact dates in connection to -- to Ahmici. So I can't remember if Ahmici took place during the Busovaca Joint Commission or during the period with the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I suggest to you that as a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission you received many complaints and that, as a matter of fact, you were flooded with complaints coming in from everywhere. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you mentioned, a lot of these complaints were based on rumours. And would it be a fair statement to say that most of the time complaints made by the HVO turned out to be rumours?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I think that the majority of the -- the rumours or the false complaints were from HVO. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I -- would it be a fair statement to say that despite the unbelievable tempo of operations during the time you were there, that you at all times received very good cooperation from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and especially from Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. And it seems that, again as I said earlier today, that we felt that there was a very close connection between Mr. Merdan and his corps commander, and Mr. Merdan seems very competent as well. So he was able to make decisions at the spot. And if he not was able to make a decision at the spot, he was very quick to resolve problems, to contact his headquarters, so we were able to solve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I'd like to move on to the kidnapping of the four HVO officers which you mentioned. You did say earlier on that it was Blaskic who informed that the HVO officers had been kidnapped and that they had been kidnapped near the front line in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that it was Ambassador Thebault who immediately set up the joint team to investigate this incident?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this team consisted of Monitor Juan Valentin from, I guess, Spain?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Spain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Merdan, Mr. Nakic, and yourself.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you've mentioned, it was HVO which believed that 7 Brigade was responsible for the kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the HVO even provided you with the name of the man they believed was driving the vehicle which was used by the kidnappers.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you checked this information, it turned out to be unfounded, because this man had already been arrested by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. And later on released, but at the time where the kidnapping took place this man was already in the custody of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, in fact, the only link with 7 Brigade at that time was because the kidnapping took place near Ravno Rostovo.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think that, and because they were operating in that area. So that's the reason for -- for them to -- to say it was the 7th Muslim Brigade. But it --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: If I might add, it was very normal that every time an incident took place, that HVO claimed that it was the 7th Muslim Brigade who was responsible for this and this and this incident, because I think that the HVO, they had -- they had respect for this unit and they -- I don't know if they were afraid for this unit, but they knew this unit were maybe better equipped, better trained than other BiH units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it was the right thing to say to whenever there's a problem to simply blame it on the 7 Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That was a very usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Whether it was true or not, it was the right thing to say for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you drove down to Ravno Rostovo, you met the commanding officer in front of the hotel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he was at that time dressed in civilian clothes, but they were Afghan style, his clothes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you saw the green banners flying in front of the hotel; that's right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you saw that those banners were green, there was some kind of Arabic script on the banners, but you never found out whether this was the real flag of 7 Brigade or not.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it could have been the real flag of 7 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It could have been the real flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know which part of 7 Brigade was in Ravno Rostovo.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Whether it was a battalion or a company or what -- what element of 7 Brigade, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you visited the hotel, you were allowed to go wherever you wanted.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you saw many soldiers, and most of them were in civilian clothes, and many wore a beard.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. But that was normal for members of the 7th Muslim Brigade to show their religion by letting their beard grow, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not speak to any of the soldiers inside, other than the commander.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall that we -- we spoke with -- with the soldiers. Maybe some of them, because we were treated very well. We have -- invited for coffee and dates and things like that. And there were some other members of the brigade that participated there, so they participated, of course, in the -- in the chat we had. But I cannot recall that we were speaking any foreign language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm what you mentioned in your statement that your impression was that this unit was not trying to hide anything?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Because they -- they showed us everything we want to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And from a military perspective, Major, can you confirm that this exact location, Ravno Rostovo Hotel, was actually a very important feature from a military perspective because it was one road leading to Bugojno and one road leading to another very important area, and that it was normal for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to have a unit at this specific location? If you can confirm.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, I think it were -- from that point of view, it was necessary to have a unit in that area to control that area. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your next stop on your search for the kidnappers was in Novi Travnik, when you briefed the HVO commander on the outcome of your visit to Ravno Rostovo.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Because it was, as I can recall, officers from his brigade that have been kidnapped. So on our way back, we want to tell him about our findings, and we told him that we have been visiting this unit from the 7th Muslim Brigade and we didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is at that point that the HVO military police came in. They wanted to arrest Merdan. And you informed them that Merdan was under your protection, and the result was that the three of you were actually arrested by the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, the three of us, we were at the office -- at the brigade commander's office. We were there. Juan went in, our interpreter and I and Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan. And it's correct that the commander of the HVO military police, he said that the only solution was to arrest Mr. Merdan, and then, as you said, we told him that Mr. Merdan were under our protection, and then he said that -- then he had to arrest us as well, and he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned to us this morning - because that was not in your statement - that this was no fun situation and this was a very, indeed, tense situation.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Because there was an armed guard beside us with his rifle, and he was -- he has taken -- he has armed his rifle, so he was able to -- to fire with the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major, you -- in this room today, you are the only soldier, other than the two accused. But can you confirm that having a loaded rife pointed at you is something that you never forget for the rest of your life and that this is indeed a very serious situation?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, we felt that it was a serious situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying, Major, that when you actually informed them after making phone calls that HVO would come and pick you up, that you were actually threatened that if HVO -- that -- sorry, if UNPROFOR comes and picks you up that they would fire at UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Because we had through our -- at that day, it was possible to phone from Novi Travnik to Zenica, so we had a telephone call to our headquarters and asked them to contact the British Battalion in Vitez and asked them to come and get us out of this. And when we told this to the military police commander, he said that if any UNPROFOR units will show up in Nova Travnik, his unit would fire at those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the end, Major, it took the intervention of Blaskic for you -- for the three of you to be released.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. And even if we had the deputy of -- of Blaskic - namely, Mr. Nakic; he was there as well - he was not able to command the military police, so he was not able to do anything. But after Colonel Blaskic had speak with the military police commander, then we were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, Major, that as a result of the kidnapping of the four HVO officers, the road between Travnik and Gornji Vakuf was blocked off by Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can remember that the road was blocked, and it was a result of the local Croats who -- they thought that they were to release -- to find anything to have a solution was too slow, so they wanted to make this blockade. And this blockade included that UNPROFOR was not able to -- to use that road, that ECMM was not able to use that road. I cannot recall that it was Blaskic who gave that order, but it was -- or it was on a local level they made this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it was a result of the kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move on to the kidnapping of Zivko Totic. You did get this information from RC Zenica that the kidnapping had just taken place. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is your colleague, Allan Laustsen, who was assigned to look into the Totic incident, and he actually attended the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the HVO actually made a videotape of the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And this video was presented to me during the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are able to confirm that throughout this investigation there was very close cooperation between the civilian police of both the HVO, the HVO side, and from the Muslim side in trying to solve this issue?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I'm not aware that there was this cooperation between those two police forces. Normally both police forces were very ineffective because they were not trained to do police work, and I cannot recall that there was a cooperation in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you aware that as a result of the Totic kidnapping all exits of Zenica were actually blocked off, that the army was told to go back to their barracks - that's both HVO and Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina - and that only the civilian police were allowed to police the town at that specific moment?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. And I think at that time, because there were two HVO brigades in Zenica but they were disarmed, and I can't remember the exact date where they were disarmed, but I think it was before that incident that they were disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will actually show you documents later --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that put the dates into perspective, because I understand that it might be difficult for you to -- to get the exact sequence of events. However, can you confirm that from a military perspective there was no gain or no incentive whatsoever for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to proceed with either the kidnapping of the four HVO officers or the kidnapping of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Because it's -- it is obvious that this was a kidnapping where the Mujahedins wanted to have something they were able to deal with. So I don't think -- and we discussed that during the investigations, that we could not see why Armija BiH should make a kidnapping like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it was also clear that this was terrorist activity, the same as those kidnapping of if two radio journalists from Radio CD?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I remember that we discussed - and it is mentioned somewhere - that the reason for the kidnapping of those two members of Radio CD should be that someone was afraid that they were able to -- using the radio system, were able to make observations for the artillery or something like that, because the Croats were -- from time to time they were shelling Zenica and then they were afraid that those Croats sitting at Radio CD were using the broadcast to -- to command the fire or to -- to tell the results of the impacts and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: All right. And if I move on to the preparation leading -- leading to the exchange. You mentioned that on the 19th of April two Mujahedin arrived at the ECMM office in Zenica and that you actually saw them arriving, and that they were dressed in Afghan-style civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And although you did not speak to them, in your statement you mentioned that they did not look like local Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned they left you with copies of a letter in both English and Bosnian and that you mentioned earlier on that it was also in German. Now, I thought I saw also a mention that there was also a French version. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It was not in Bosnian; it was in German.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: German. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: English and German --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, you're right. I made a mistake from reading my notes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It's correct that there maybe were a copy in French as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: But I haven't mentioned that, because I was in doubt. But it could be in French as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my colleague from the Prosecution actually showed -- showed you a letter earlier on, and he drew your attention to the handwritten part. And that's actually the only paper you've ever seen was the handwritten part.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the typed version, or if there were any, you never saw that.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Can I have that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You never saw the same letter put into typewriter.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the -- they left you a contact name at least - they left maybe you or someone else within ECMM - and the contact name was someone called Abu Haris, and they also gave you a phone number. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that phone number you could tell had nothing to do with any number in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I don't know, because I didn't participate in -- in the meetings where they were going to have all those negotiations. But I can recall we had a contact name and there was a telephone number, but I don't know if this telephone number was a local number in Zenica or it was somewhere else. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's perfectly okay. We have other witnesses who can --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- confirm this, so I thank you for your -- for your answer. Now, after you had informed the HVO of this situation as well as the civilian police and the ICRC, the HVO was requested to provide the names of the Mujahedin or - that's what you put in your report - of the foreign citizens that they were holding in custody because the ICRC wanted to go and see these people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We had a list of names from the Arabic Group, and we asked HVO to make a list to see who they had detained of foreign persons. I can remember that we then make a compilation between those two lists to see if the names from the -- the Arabic list were similar to the list from -- from HVO, to see if it's correct that those people --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That they were holding those people.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yeah. And I can remember there was a little discussion about the names of -- of the detained persons, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you are able to confirm, Major, that there is a difference between a foreign national citizen and the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's why -- it's very confusing, because sometimes we use the word "Mujahedin"; sometimes we use "member of the Arabic Group"; sometimes we use "foreign citizens." So it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But they don't necessarily mean the same thing, and sometimes those terms could be used on and on without really pinpointing a specific name to a person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the HVO did provide you with this list and when the ICRC tried to gain access to see those people, the HVO accepted but the Mujahedin refused.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. But I can only recall this because I have later on read the report from Dieter Schellschmidt. I did not participate myself in the negotiations and in the meetings, so it's difficult to -- for me to -- to say if it's true or not. I only have it from -- from the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can -- you can -- because this is in your statement, you can confirm that because the Mujahedin had refused, there was an exchange of letters and a video which was given to ECMM.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your statement, you mention that the letters for the four officers were actually given to someone in Travnik, who then brought it to ECMM.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's probably correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the letters in reference -- in relation to Totic, there were two letters - that's after the initial one, of course - two letters; one addressed to Blaskic and one addressed to Sakic, that both of these letters were addressed to ECMM. They were given to ECMM.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that throughout these preparations some Mujahedin and some HVO visited the ECMM office on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that on one occasion only Allan Laustsen had to deal with these Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. I can recall one meeting with one representative from the Arabic Group and Allan Laustsen dealt with this guy, and I can remember that -- because all ECMM monitors were having our identity card in front of us on a chain around our neck, and because we were very proud to be Danes, the Danish monitor, we had a Danish flag on the -- on the -- not on the front side but on the other side of the identity card, ID card, and suddenly Allan Laustsen's card turned round so the Mujahedin -- or the Arabic, the member of the Arabic Group, he saw this Danish flag and then he was able to address him in a few Danish words, saying -- translated to English, "Hell, are you Danish?" But he was only able to speak a few Danish words, but it shows that they were people experienced [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major, you did mention something earlier on. You said on one hand that you did not take part in all those meetings, but you did say that you were aware that when the Mujahedin showed up in front of the hotel where you lived, Hotel Internacional, that the civilian BiH police disappeared and that's why at times they were allowed to go into that room with their own weapons.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. The local police, they were afraid of these Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can confirm, Major, that both the local police, as well as all the population, they were very scared of these people?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In fact, you can confirm, Major, that soldiers were afraid, as well as all members of the International Community. You didn't feel good if you saw one of those people around. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, we didn't feel secure when we were in -- in areas where we knew that the Mujahedins were operating. And sometimes they made their own checkpoints, checkpoints that had not been coordinated with the -- the 3rd Corps. And sometimes on those checkpoints -- it was only temporary checkpoints. Sometimes they -- they had their head covered by this balaclava. And we have heard rumours that when they were having this balaclava on, they were on a special mission doing naughty things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you thought about those people, Major, am I right in saying that the word that went through your mind at that time was the word "terrorist" and not "soldier"?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We saw them not as soldiers but more like terrorists. It seemed to us that the Mujahedins were out of control, that they were fighting their own war in the war, and I can remember that General Hadzihasanovic mentioned that, because I discussed that briefly during a meeting where he said that the Mujahedins were harming the Bosnian representation, that the Mujahedins were fighting, as I said, their own war within the war, and it was difficult for the Armija BiH to control what the Mujahedins were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I move to the exchange, Major, can you confirm that the plan was, as drafted up by the ECMM, to have a simultaneous exchange in Travnik, in Kaonik, and in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you mentioned that you were in Travnik and that your work was to receive the four HVO officers and then to take them from the Mujahedin and to take these four officers back to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. When they were released, we took them in the vehicle from -- the armoured vehicle from BritBat and we took them to Hotel Vitez, where General -- Colonel Blaskic has his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you actually gave those four officers to Colonel Blaskic, he actually made a big media thing out of this and he congratulated you in front of everyone, saying, "Yea, yea, yea, Mr. Baggesen."

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yeah. He used it as some PR, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Mr. Morsink, who will come and testify here, was at Kaonik. You can confirm that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in Zenica, you mentioned that Mr. Schellschmidt was there. Is it possible that Mr. Landry was also in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I would like -- I would like to ask my learned friend from the Defence to not mention any names of witnesses who are likely to come at a later point in time for the obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are going to take a break. It is quarter to 6.00. And we shall resume at five past 6.00, and we shall work until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another 55 minutes. I hope that Mr. Bourgon will proceed rapidly, because it might be necessary for others to ask questions, the Judges, the Prosecution. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major Bagessen, before the break, we were discussing quickly the exchange in Zenica, but you confirmed that you were not in Zenica for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And whatever you heard about this exchange concerning the machine-guns and the weapons used and the people that were there, you saw none of that.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No. I just heard it from -- from Dieter Schellschmidt and the other colleagues that were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know whether the monitor Landry was in Zenica or not.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember where he was that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you can recall that all of this issue with the exchange was indeed a very tense exchange that monopolises all of the attention of ECMM for at least the duration of that day.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will move on to another topic, which is when you are appointed to chair the joint humanitarian commission. And am I right in saying that this commission was born on the 10th of June as part of a cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that it is Ambassador Thebault who assigned you to chair this commission?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that as part of this commission you visited all detention facilities in that area?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to go into the music school. We've heard about that. But I'd like to ask you that there were as chairman of this commission allegations were communicated to you by the HVO that there was another school or engineering school of some type where the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were detaining people and that you actually went there and that it was totally unfounded.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I can't remember -- it was a sort of school. I can't remember. I think it's correct that it was called the engineer school or something like that. But it was -- it was a school in Zenica and we went to that spot, and there was no evidence there that there have been any detained persons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were also informed by the HVO about people detained in Mehurici, and you went there on the 23rd of June with a BritBat escort, with a Warrior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It's correct that we went with a BritBat escort. I cannot remember if it was with this vehicle called Warrior or what type of vehicles we had with us, but it was some armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you can confirm, Major, that on your way to Mehurici there were two members of the -- two HVO members of your commission who were caught in an ambush in HVO territory, close to Vitez, and that one of the two was killed and that the other was injured? Can you confirm this event?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you were told and you believed that the Mujahedin were responsible for this because it was in HVO territory.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It's correct that it was the opinion of the -- of the HVO that this ambush against the commission was -- was carried out by the Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Mehurici, you visited the school there with the commanding officer of the facility, and there were a number of civilians, and you mentioned in your statement that the commanding officer told you that he was holding onto those civilians to protect them from the Mujahedin. Is that what the commander told you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That was what he told us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew that there were actually Mujahedin in the area of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We knew that, and we later on the same day, during our visit there, I had a contact from my driver, [indiscernible], and he told us that he, together with the BritBat escort were surrounded by members of Mujahedins and that those members of the Mujahedins were aiming their anti-tank weapons, RPG 7, against our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's when -- you got this communication as you were inside the school.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's when you requested the commanding officer of that school to at least get you out of this trouble by speaking to the Mujahedin who were pointing their anti-tank weapons as your vehicles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I asked him to do something to -- to solve that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again, this is not one of those make-up situations; this was real life, having anti-tank weapons pointed at you, and the commander of the Mehurici school had a very loud and tense argument with the leader of the Mujahedin and he succeeded in getting them to leave.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you asked him about who were these people, he told you that these are dangerous Mujahedin and that they were not his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And now, with respect to the people who were detained - because you were in that school - you were able to say, and you confirmed in your statement that these people were well treated.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: "Well treated," that's maybe a big word, but during the circumstances, we think that they were well treated. We spoke with them and they said, "Okay, we have something to drink, we have something to eat. We can have fresh air." They had problems with -- with the toilet and things like that, but that was the situation everywhere where we came to see detained persons, that normally they were treated well. Not -- they could be better, but it could be worse as well. But it seems that they were maybe not in the best shape but they were in good shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major, you and I will agree that of course this was not Holiday Inn, but that in the circumstances you actually can attest that they were treated better than could be expected under those hard and difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at the responsibility of a commander with respect to people who are detained, you can confirm with me that of course every commander up the chain of command is responsible for people who are detained.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that of course the responsibility is different at different levels.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that a situation like you saw in Mehurici, you would not expect the corps commander to take his car and drive down to Mehurici to find out himself what is going on there.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No. But we would expect that the corps commander had given his units some directive how to behave and how to behave in connection to the Geneva Conventions and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you would expect that a commander would issue instructions to abide by the Geneva Conventions and unless he gets information to the contrary by his own subordinates, then you don't expect him to look out whether to see if violations are committed. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for a commander to know things, what the situation are in the area if no one tells him what the situation is. But as you said, it is not necessary for the commander to -- to visit the spot, but he is still responsible. He can give some directives. And he can assure that someone are taken care in controlling that this directive are fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I object against this line of questioning. My learned friend from the Defence is asking the witness, who is a fact witness, questions which should be asked -- which an expert should be asked. There's a huge difference between the situations we had in the past that we asked a fact witness, based on his knowledge and based what he had seen and experienced, to draw conclusions. This time my learned friend from the Defence is asking the witness not based on what he himself has seen or experienced but asks him purely questions which are of a nature that only an expert can testify about. Therefore, I object against this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber was following the question put to the witness. Mr. Bourgon asked the witness, who is a commander - don't forget that we have an officer here - he asked him about the responsibilities of a commander. He is nevertheless in a position to answer such a question. And, Mr. Withopf, I do not see how this could be a problematic question, given that we have an officer here who mentioned the Geneva Conventions himself. Mr. Baggesen, you have listened to the objection. You're an officer. Imagine a situation which you would have to govern a prison with soldiers under your orders. In such a case, would you have given orders, instructions, to your guards, to the wardens -- to your guards with respect to the Geneva Conventions? This is the type of question we could ask you, since you are an officer. What could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I should have detained persons in my custody, I have to assure that the subordinates that are commanding this facility, that they knew about the Geneva Conventions, that they knew how to behave. And if I'm not in the position to go to a spot myself, I can ask another one to -- to have this control at the facility, but I would still have the responsibility because I'm the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... General Hadzihasanovic, of which you were a witness, that with his responsibilities with respect to Mehurici, that he would still be responsible but what you expect of him is different than what you expect from the commanding officer that you met on the ground. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the situation of General Hadzihasanovic, you visited the detention facility KP Dom, did you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you understand that this was like a corps-level detention facility.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I think that the prison in Zenica was a prison as well before the conflict and during the conflict it was used by the local authorities, as well as it was used by the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it would be normal in your -- based on your experience, it would be normal for General Hadzihasanovic to pay more attention to KP Dom because it was where all the people would be eventually transferred, if there was a need to do so.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I don't know the chain of command in -- in this prison world, but I could imagine that this detention facility was closer related to the corps than, for example, the before-mentioned school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I'll move on to another issue, and that is the situation on the ground and relating to how difficult the situation was. Now, I would like to begin by talking about the situation on 21 of April. In your statement, you mentioned that there were allegations that Croat villages had been attacked and that you went there with your colleague Junhov and with Father Stipan Radic, and that you concluded that there was little damage, although some houses had been looted and the owners had left. Can you confirm this episode?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you also confirm that at that time there were lots of rumours circulating that the ABiH was planning a big operation against the Croats and that rumours were everywhere about what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you also confirm that on 25 April yourself, your colleague Morsink, and again Father Stipan, visited the villages of Janjac, Susanj, Stranjani, Dolac, and Konjevici, and that your conclusion was that the properties were intact, although many had been looted? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can confirm that I visited a lot of villages. I cannot remember sitting here the names and I cannot remember the dates, but I can remember I've been visiting those -- a lot of Croat villages together with Henk Morsink and -- and Father Stipan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you recall that on this specific occasion -- and I know you don't recall, maybe this will bring back some memories to you -- that the Muslim villagers wanted the Croats to return there and that you thought it was safe enough for them to return?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. One -- the reason for us to bring Father Stipan with us, because we want to use Father Stipan to be the one that was doing this fact-finding together with us, so he was able to tell the Croats that it was safe for them to return to the villages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that you saw the BiH police arresting looters and that this made you feel good because it would be something that Father Stipan could report back to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that most of the refugees in fact returned but that initially it was the HVO who tried to stop them, even by firing in the air to scare them not to come back?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. In the beginning, when we were trying to take all the refugees back to the villages, we went to the area together with some buses from the local Red Cross. At a checkpoint the HVO took the buses from us, because they were using the buses to -- to move the refugees to a Croat-dominated area. And I can remember I think it was almost 2.000 refugees. And we succeeded to manage the return of 1.600, I think. The rest were already -- been moved by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Major, that on 20 April you visited KP Dom with your colleague Landry and that you noticed that the conditions were good, that one man was released because he had some kind of surgery and you thought that it was not good for him to stay there, but that overall people were well treated as KP Dom? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: You used the word "Holiday Inn" before. It was not Holiday Inn, but they were treated as you could -- better than you could expect, and it's correct that there was one older man who had been through an operation for some throat cancer, in the throat, and we asked him to be released, and because he was not a criminal, because we were -- we were not -- if it was persons who were detained or imprisoned because they were criminals, they should stay in the prison; but this man was only there because he was a Croat. So he was released at the spot, without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Major, that you went back several times to KP Dom and that it was all -- the situation was always as good as what you just described?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Major, that this was very different from what you could see when you visited HVO prisons, such as Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I think -- you are mentioning Kaonik. That was the worst example you can -- you could take, because the detained persons in Kaonik were not treated that good compared to the other places we visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Major, that it is from your statement, also from a various of reports, that in Zenica there was shelling -- artillery shelling on and off almost every other day, that this made it very difficult for both the population, for yourself as a monitor, and for the headquarters of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It was very difficult working conditions to us, because we have to work in that environment, and of course it was difficult for the civilian population that we were shelled almost every second day, as you said. Sometimes it was a shelling from HVO. This was not proved through the Blaskic case but it was our findings. And later on the Bosnian Serb army started to shell that area. And the Bosnian Serb army were shelling Croat positions as well as at -- at BiH positions, trying to -- to make a conflict between those two, because it looked like the BiH were shelling HVO and it looked like the HVO were shelling the -- the BiH, but through our findings we were able to tell them that it was not the opposite party who was shelling them but it was the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Major, that people died as a result of this shelling and more specifically on one occasion the marketplace was shelled and 13 people died? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I confirm that was the first attack in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to what was the situation on the other side, if I may use this expression. In terms of what the -- what was going on in Muslim villages. Did you visit any Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can confirm that if we compare the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the first case this army, was your impression - and that again is from your statement - that they had decided, based on the Vance Owen Peace Plan, to basically do what the plan called for by force and by grabbing the land which was at that point occupied by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. It seems like HVO legalised their ethnic cleansing because they want to have the Croat-dominated provinces ethnically cleaned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So -- thank you, Major. And you are familiar with some of the actions of the HVO; namely, in Ahmici, which is probably the biggest massacre that took place during the time you were there.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I mention to you some towns -- for example, you recall visiting on the 28th of April the local Red Cross in Visoko? Do you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your statement provided in 1996, you mentioned that there were thousands of refugees coming from the following towns: Svinjarevo, Jehovac, Gromiljak, Behrici, Gomionica, Bilalovac, to name but a few. Are you familiar with these names?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that refugees came from these towns.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. And I can remember in that report I made that we had those figures so we know how many refugees there were from the different communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Major, on the 29th of April, you made a visit with Team Z1, and I quote from your statement here, in terms of: "Our findings were that in Polje Visnjica most of the Muslims had been burned and all the Muslims had left the village, but there were still Croats families in the village." Is that -- do you recall stating this in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to Hercezi, you say 14 Muslims were killed in the area. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you recall that in Visnjica 40 houses were burned and five Muslim men were killed in the field? Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in Gomionica you had no problems visiting the village with the HVO. The village was abandoned and all the Muslim houses were totally destroyed: "Yet we were not surprised when we saw Croat houses without any damage in the village." Can you recall this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you also recall that you also saw HVO regular soldiers and some snipers from the HVO pursuing your team while doing this visit?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes. And actually, we had -- as I recall it, Gomionica was the village situated north of Kiseljak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: And we had actually problems to get in there the first day, because the HVO denied us access to Gomionica. We tried again the next day. I was there together with an escort from the Canadian Battalion. And at that time the platoon commander and I, we were shot at from HVO positions, and we succeeded to -- to get out again. So it was the third day we tried to get into Gomionica, where there was no problem. And at that day, we saw that patrols from HVO were trying to come close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Can you recall that when you were in Central Bosnia the issue of communications, and I'm talking about the PTT. You report in this statement that the engineer you spoke to actually was perfectly able to re-establish the telephone lines, for example, between Sarajevo and Zenica or Travnik and Zenica, but that he refused to do so without an order from Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We had a problem with the PTT line between Zenica and Sarajevo, and at that time my team was ordered to try to do some fact-finding to see what we can do. And we found in Kiseljak one of the Croat engineers who was responsible for the PTT line, and in the beginning he said it was destroyed because the PTT building in Kiseljak were destroyed, but we didn't find any impacts or anything destroyed at this PTT building. So we had a conversation with this man again. Then he said that -- that the PTT line between Zenica and Sarajevo were cut down, and he didn't see -- he didn't see it was necessary for the Muslims in Zenica to have contact with the Muslims in Sarajevo, and the only one who could order him to reopen the line were Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. One last question, and I'd like to quickly show you some documents. The -- you mentioned simply spontaneously a little earlier your conversation with General Hadzihasanovic concerning the Mujahedin and how he felt about the Mujahedin. Can you confirm that on this occasion General Hadzihasanovic also mentioned to you that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not strong enough to fight the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I can't remember if he mentioned the whole Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but as far as I remember he was thinking on his own corps level that he not was able to -- to control and maybe disarm the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I'd like to show you now some -- some documents. And I would simply ask you to recognise the documents, because we don't have time to go into it. But these are your own reports that you produced as a monitor in Bosnia. So there are a series of reports that I would like for -- simply for you to identify simply as being your own reports of what you talked about, what you saw during your time in Bosnia. So if I go with you. There is a report dated 28th of April, and this is signed "Lars Baggesen." Do you recognise this as being your report?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And moving to the next page is also another daily report dated 29th of April, and at the end we see "regards, Allan Laustsen," who was your colleague, and yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At paragraph 4 we say the team conclusion stating that: "It is obvious that an ethnic cleansing had taken place in the area." Can you confirm that you are talking about the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next page is a report on 9th of May, 1993. And again, this one is signed by yourself -- or at least, it says "Lars Baggesen." And your colleague Stavros Kinigopoulos.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's my Greek colleague. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this was your -- this was your investigation on the origin of the shelling in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next one is on the 12th of May, and again talks about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it talks about -- sorry, I'll move to the next one quickly. On the 16th of May, the next page, and again this is signed by yourself, Lars Baggesen, and Bent Faerge. I don't know who which individual is. Can you confirm who this individual is?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, Bent Faerge is a Danish monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm at paragraph 6 of this report that Mr. Merdan and Mr. Skopljak agreed to release all civilians who had been in prison in Kaonik and Zenica and to release all of the members of the ABiH imprisoned in Busovaca and all those of the HVO imprisoned in Zenica after May 17th.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that what happened in fact is that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina released all the Croats but that the HVO did not release all of the members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall this fact?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall that fact, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I move on to the next report dated 18th May. This one talks about Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's a two-page report, and again signed by you. Now, you were in Maglaj and in the Zepce-Maglaj area and Zavidovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this was, from the strategic point of view, a very important area which should have attracted the attention of the corps commander simply because if he lost that area, he would be cut off from the north?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, and the situation in that area were very tense, because the whole area were surrounded by the Bosnian Serb army and it was under a daily attack and it was -- the Bosnian army was very close to succeeding to cut off that area from the rest of the area of responsibility for the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Major, that in this specific area there was initially cooperation between the HVO and the ABiH and that the big problem around June was that the HVO was pulling out and there were very strong sides of cooperation between the HVO and the VRS, which made the situation of General Hadzihasanovic all that much more difficult?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It's correct that there was good cooperation between BiH and HVO. It seems to us there was a good cooperation. And we heard about rumours and we -- I think we have -- we find some facts as well that there were cooperation between the HVO and the Bosnian Serb army as well. And it made some tensions in the cooperation between HVO and BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the cooperation between the Army of VRS and the HVO, you were also aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I was not aware if there was cooperation between the -- what are they called, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yeah, between the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the HVO. That they were -- there were strong signs that they were cooperating together, and as a matter of fact the HVO were withdrawing from the line, which made the situation of General Hadzihasanovic difficult.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We knew that they were replacing some of the HVO units in that area were -- withdrawal, and reorganised in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we move to your last report on this -- in this bundle, Major, the 26th of June. This is ones that part of your joint humanitarian commission. Can I draw your attention to paragraph 3, in terms of the number of prisoners released during that time. Are you able to confirm that only 190 Muslims were released, as opposed to 453 Croats?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's not the next but the next again. From the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yeah. And the reason for that were that there were more Croats detained than Muslims. I can remember we had a discussion, and actually the two members -- the two members from BiH in the joint humanitarian commission was -- was a little afraid of their life because they have been threatened and their families have been threatened because the commission was releasing more Croats and -- than Muslims, because those -- or one of those members from the Armija BiH were Croat by birth, he was threatened by the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Major, one last question on this document: The last paragraph of the first page, where it is mentioned that a Mr. Stjepan Siber from the ABiH, that because they were both Croats --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: They were both Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- the HVO rep was a Croat and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina representative was also a Croat, and that for this reason Mr. Siber wanted to release all the Croats, and that is also a reason why there were more Croats released. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
