utterances.text: No. I think the reason that there were more Croats released than Muslims were because there were more detained persons by -- of Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender a series of documents under one number. The witness has identified these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, about the witness's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, there is no objection of the Prosecution; however, I wish to note that my learned friend has forgotten the document of the 23rd of June, 1993, and in order to not make things complicated, the Prosecution is not objecting against tendering this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar, can you give me a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is going to be DH167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, we have another quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you very much, Major Bagessen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, do you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Major Bagessen, only a few questions on behalf of Mr. Kubura. It's correct that you cannot recall whether you ever had the opportunity to meet Mr. Kubura, who was the acting commander of the 7th Brigade at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You did meet some soldiers from the 7th Brigade you said in your evidence in chief in the music school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But you also said in your evidence that none of these soldiers spoke a foreign language, Arabic in particular.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We were only speaking with -- with people who were speaking the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So you never heard any Arabic spoken in the music school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: The soldiers there allowed you to inspect the entire music school, with the exception of one room you said, where they said there were communications.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And you saw some cables going into that room.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Once you -- you heard that and saw those cables, would it be correct that you understood to some extent why there had been some difficulty in getting access to the music school in the first place, because of the communications that were there?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No, I don't think that was the reason that we were denied access. I simply think that -- that the local commander did not have the -- the guards or the responsibility to -- to let us in and he needs an order for higher level -- for higher level, despite the fact that I have had this piece of paper telling him that -- telling them that I have access to all compounds in Bosnia. But I think he needs to have this confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So he wanted to make sure, the soldier who you spoke to there.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But you can confirm that communications and where they were located was a sensitive matter for both sides in the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You said in your evidence in chief that you would have been suspicious if you were not shown a particular room, with the exception of the communications room.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And that you therefore presume that you saw all the rooms in the music school, from the basement all the way up through all the floors.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise you, would it, Major Bagessen, that the music school was not in fact the headquarters of the 7th Brigade; the headquarters were elsewhere in a place called Bilmiste?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: It would not surprise me, because it was normal when we were having meetings with people that if we had a meeting with someone from -- from the 7th Muslim Brigade or from another brigade, everyone was, as I said before, calling themselves commander. But you can be a commander on different levels, and commanders on different levels have their headquarters. So when we are referring to that there was a headquarter from 7th Muslim Brigade at the music school, it -- it's not necessarily a big headquarters. It could maybe be a company headquarter or -- I know that a platoon don't have a headquarter like that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: -- but it could be their post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But did you know that the brigade headquarters were at Bilmiste at the time?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall the -- the position of the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You never had any reason to go to that place to meet with the 7th Brigade, did you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I didn't have any reason to do that, and I don't know if any of my colleagues went to the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You never met any commanders of the 7th Brigade at the brigade headquarters in Bilmiste, did you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I have never been at that headquarters, but I did meet some other commanders on a different level, maybe battalion commanders, but I cannot recall their names or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: At the music school, once you had searched through the -- the whole building, you did not find any detainees kept at the music school when you were there, did you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: The 7th Brigade units, in your view, were some of the most disciplined forces operating in Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: To my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: The HVO, however, you say, claimed that there was a link between these forces and the Mujahedin and the kidnappings that you've testified about today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But in your evidence in chief, you have said that you didn't see any link between the 7th Brigade and the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: No. The only link we saw was the discussion about this vehicle that the messengers have been used. Later on it was observed in front of one of the 7 Muslim Brigade's compounds. I will not use now the word "headquarters." But it was observed. And I can't remember if it was in front of the music school or in front of the compound in Ravno Rostovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: This was a vehicle that you yourself didn't see, but it was a discussion that you had with your colleagues about the matter.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember if I saw the vehicle myself, but I can remember the discussion. But I cannot remember if I saw it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And even though it's just one small story about what was happening at the time, it's not a matter that you can confirm in your evidence today firsthand; you didn't see the vehicle in these different places that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, we had a discussion about this vehicle, that it has been observed the two places, but I cannot recall if I saw it myself. I just heard it from the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Continuing with this allegation of this link. I'm not sure if you're aware, but Mr. Totic himself testified in this trial in public session about the kidnappings. Did you on any occasion interview him after the incident?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: From what you knew at the time and from the documents that we've seen today, it would be correct to say, would it not, that the Mujahedin were the force that ran the entire show when it came to these exchanges? They were the ones making the demands; they were the ones drawing up the lists of their people to be exchanged; they were the ones involved in the meetings and the negotiations and indeed the exchanges themselves in May.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You were referred earlier on by my learned friend for the Prosecution to a report prepared by Mr. Schellschmidt. And in paragraph 10 of that report, which he took you to - I'm not going to give it to you again - but you did confirm that it was in fact the Mujahedin who demanded a meeting with the HVO, the 7th Brigade, and a number of other organisations in -- in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So the allegations that were made by the HVO, then, would you agree with me that they proved to be wholly incorrect and in fact the 7th Brigade was not involved at all in the perpetration of these kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN
utterances.text: We didn't see any link between the 7th Muslim Brigade and the kidnappings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major Bagessen. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, any re-examination on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have a number of issues to address which result from the cross-examination. And I'm aware of the time that has passed by. I don't know whether it deems appropriate to start the re-examination now and to continue tomorrow or to leave it for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may continue today, but how much time will you need all together?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have five distinct areas to address, and I anticipate that I may need some 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall then continue tomorrow, because if you take 20 minutes, there may be some additional questions on the part of the Defence. Major, unfortunately, you will have to spend the night in The Hague and come back tomorrow, because the Judges will also have some questions to put to you. We were not able to finish your testimony today. I would kindly ask you to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'm now going to ask Madam Registrar [as interpreted] to accompany you out of the courtroom, and I would like to finish by asking you not to have any contacts with any of the parties. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, you last week asked the parties -- you last week asked the parties to discuss the issue of the documents which were shown by Defence to the military expert and which the Prosecution wishes to be tendered as Prosecution exhibits. The parties have discussed this issue, and the parties are in agreement that these documents should be tendered into evidence, should be tendered now, but should be tendered as Defence exhibits, Defence exhibits for the accused Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Bourgon, that was DH153 and -- to 164 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was DH154 [as interpreted] which was in class A in English until DH163. In any case, there are two corrections that we have to make before we tender these documents. In the Exhibit Number 156, one document has to be withdrawn. It has already been admitted as document number 66, DH66. The date is 8 June 1993, and the number of the document is 19-8/02-230-150. The document was addressed to the district military prosecutor and it was admitted during the testimony of witness Ivkic on 18 March 2004. We would like to withdraw this document in English, number 3. As far as the document DH163 is concerned -- I'm sorry. I apologise. There is an additional document which doesn't have a number yet which is in English 11 class 8 -- English 11, binder A. There is a series of documents there which have already been admitted through Mr. Ivkic's testimony. But there is one additional document in English; the date is 11 March 1993. The title is, "The request for information on criminal charges." The centre was the 3rd Corps, and it was sent to all the units. This document bears the number 04/739-1. This document -- we need an additional number for this document in order to be able to tender this document into evidence. And finally, Mr. President, I would like to say that there were documents that were tendered without prejudice to the Defence concerning the arguments that we are going to present about the admissibility of documents. We propose to propose [as interpreted] certain documents into evidence, but now we don't have any objections to the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to the documents that have been marked for identification, agreement was reached and the documents can be admitted into evidence, with the exception of the document that must be withdrawn, DH66. It has already been admitted. In English number 11, there is a document dated the 11th of March, 1993, and you would like this document to be provided with an additional number. The number will therefore be DH165. Mr. Registrar, is that correct? What will the exhibit number be for the additional document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the number will be DH168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The number will be 168. And the others, marked for identification, will be admitted and given definitive exhibit numbers. Tomorrow we will continue with the hearing of this witness, and we also have another witness available for tomorrow. There is a slight problem as far as the premises are concerned. We should be in Courtroom II tomorrow, and that's where we should be throughout the week. Does this cause the Defence any problems, given the model?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we won't be using the model with the witness who will be appearing here on Thursday, but we do want to use the map, so it would be better if possible to be in Courtroom III or even in Courtroom I, in order to be able to use the map. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have no problems as far as tomorrow is concerned, but I'll ask the registrar whether it might be possible to have a hearing in Courtroom III, although we are scheduled to be in Courtroom II. But you will see what the situation is. I think that Blagojevic is supposed to be in that courtroom, but that is something that you should look into. If there are no other questions, I would like to invite everyone to appear for the hearing that will start tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
